title: Page-folding memory sampling sprint notes
body:
Context and motivation:

We observed sustained tail-latency spikes on multi-tenant hosts when large sequence-length requests co-occur with high-concurrency small-seq requests. Hypothesis: page-folding (logical grouping of physical pages during large-kv writes/reads) interacts poorly with our sampling/eviction logic and artificially inflates observed reuse entropy, causing unnecessary paging and memory-bandwidth pressure.

Goals for this sprint:
- Build lightweight microsampler that captures page-level access density over short windows (100ms, 500ms, 2s).
- Measure correlation between page-folding events (big model checkpoints, large-batch KV fills) and sudden drops in reuse-rate.
- Validate if subtle alignment shifts across NUMA nodes increase DMA stall counts.
- Propose a mitigation (fold-detection + local-hold window) and run A/B on a canary host.

Experimental design:
- Environment: r5-gpu-large hosts (8x A100-sim), Linux 5.19, 2-socket, numa enabled.
- Workloads: mix of two synthetic traces:
  * Long-seq generator: 8–12k tokens, bursty (1s on / 9s off), high KV churn (fills ~30% of KV bucket).
  * Micro-seq generator: 8–256 tokens, steady 200 qps.
- Sampler: kernel-probe style userland microtracer (probing page faults + explicit cache metadata ops). Sampling rates: 10Hz, 20Hz, 100Hz.
- Metrics captured: page-hotness (accesses/page-window), reuse-rate (per-key, 1s/10s windows), eviction-counts/s, page-split events (pages migrated across slab or NUMA boundary), memory read GB/s, DMA waits (cycles), P50/P95/P99 latencies for both request classes.

Key findings (summary):
1) Short windows (100ms) show clear spike in page-hotness at the start of long-seq bursts. The spike contains a high fraction of sequential page reads that then decay over ~400ms.
2) Our standard sampling (10Hz) misses the initial microburst in ~37% of runs. 100Hz captures it reliably and shows a median 1.6x higher instantaneous memory read GB/s during the first 300ms of the burst.
3) When burst begins, reuse-rate for the micro-seq class drops by 18–26% (median across hosts) for ~600ms, causing their P95 latency to increase 2.1x.
4) We observed page-split/migrate events increasing 3x during bursts on cross-node allocations (NUMA local -> remote), aligned with elevated DMA wait cycles.
5) Eviction count spikes are concentrated on a small set (~12%) of KV buckets that overlap with the long-seq's prefix keys; this indicates fold-alignment rather than uniform churn.

Detailed observations:
- Timing: in most cases the sequence is: long-seq request arrives -> runtime allocates large contiguous KV regions -> prefetch warms some pages -> immediate sequential accesses trigger kernel-level page-table updates -> sampling shows a high contiguous-run access pattern -> eviction policy quickly demotes LRU candidates that micro-seq relied on -> micro-seq latency rises.
- Bandwidth numbers: baseline host idle read BW ~145 GB/s (measured); during captured bursts read BW peaks at 210–235 GB/s for 120–350ms depending on sampler alignment. Sustained BW over 1s increases by ~12% overall.
- DMA stalls: cross-node migration increases DMA stall counters by ~2.8x during peak compared to baseline.
- Sampling impact: 100Hz sampling added ~2.3% CPU overhead on the runtime manager thread; 20Hz ~0.6%. All sampling runs negligible impact to request latencies when sampler is isolated to control plane thread.

Hypotheses and root-cause reasoning:
- Page-folding: when the runtime writes or reserves pages for a large prefix, the kernel (or allocator) tends to group physical pages in contiguous chunks which end up mapped to the same memory channel. This creates temporary hot channels and accelerates eviction pressure elsewhere.
- Sampling/eviction window mismatch: our eviction TTLs are tuned for longer windows (seconds), so short sharp spikes cause reactive evictions that are not beneficial once the burst subsides — we evict then immediately regret (thrashing).
- NUMA misalignment: large allocations without explicit node pinning sometimes get split and migrated causing extra DMA traffic, exacerbating bandwidth pressure and tail spikes.

Mitigation ideas tried during sprint (A/B candidates):
A) Fold-detect hold: detect contiguous-sequence access patterns and insert a local hold window (400–800ms) on candidate pages so they are deprioritized for eviction until the burst finishes.
B) Short-term TTL bump: dynamically increase retention score for pages that show >X accesses in <Y ms, avoiding premature eviction.
C) NUMA-aware allocator path: for long-seq allocations, prefer local NUMA slab and mark as "bulk" to avoid incremental migration.
D) Prefetch-smoothing: instead of aggressive bulk prefetch, stagger prefetches across micro-batches to avoid synchronized channel saturation.

Results of quick A/B run (canary host):
- A (fold-detect hold 600ms): micro-seq P95 reduction back to within 1.05x baseline in 82% of trials; long-seq median latency increased by ~4% (acceptable). Bandwidth peaks reduced by ~18% on average.
- B (short-term TTL bump): similar behavioral improvement but with slightly higher memory footprint (+3%).
- C (NUMA pinning): eliminated many DMA stall spikes but introduced occasional allocation failures on highly fragmented hosts; needs allocator fallbacks.
- D (prefetch-smoothing): promising in simulation but required larger changes to prefetch pipeline; not tested in canary.

Open questions / unknowns:
- Best TTL/hold values for mixed tenant patterns — current 400–800ms is heuristic from these traces. Need wider traffic variety (real traffic replay).
- Interaction with multi-tenant fairness policies: holding pages may affect tenant quotas. Policy mismatch risk.
- Effects on long-running models with persistent hot prefixes (SFT / RLHF models) — could be beneficial or harmful depending on long-term working set.
- Fragmented-host behavior with NUMA pinning requires allocator improvements or fallback-first approach.

Next steps / action items:
- E1: Run controlled 24h replay of production traces (PR replay ID: PR#5123) with A and B active on 3 canaries (owners: Ethan, Mariana). Due: 2026-02-20.
- E2: Add lightweight fold detector to runtime telemetry and surface as a Console alert (metric: fold_peak_ratio). Owner: Jonah. Due: 2026-02-18.
- E3: Check allocator patch to add explicit NUMA "bulk" path and fallback path for fragmented hosts (RFC + unit tests). Owner: Priya. Due: 2026-03-01.
- E4: Evaluate policy-within-rolling-updates: ensure tenant fairness constraints not violated during hold windows. Owner: Eng-Policy. Due: 2026-03-08.

Quick todos (developer scratch):
- Instrument page-split event with stack traces and log a hashed prefix key for offline correlation (low-overhead sampling).
- Add microbenchmark that can synthetic reproduce fold-alignment (single process that allocates large contiguous kv and touches in decreasing stride).
- Surface the sample-capture as flame graphs for the 0–500ms window for easier debugging.

Notes to reviewers:
- This doc is rough; experimental numbers vary by host and kernel build. Please annotate any edge cases you see or ask for raw traces (we have perf.data tarballs linked in PR#5123).
- If we converge on a remediation, we should prepare a short playbook for SRE on how to toggle the hold window and rollback safely.

Appendix: quick numbers table (medians across 12 runs)
- micro-sampler rate: 100Hz capture ratio: 99%
- median micro-seq P95 baseline: 42ms -> burst P95: 89ms (fold event)
- fold-hold (600ms) micro-seq P95 during burst: 44ms
- median read BW baseline: 145 GB/s -> peak: 225 GB/s without mitigation -> 185 GB/s with fold-hold
- DMA stall cycles: baseline: 1.2M -> burst: 3.4M -> with NUMA pin: 1.3M

References and links:
- PR#5123 (trace replay and raw perf tarballs)
- JIRA-RT-1423 (incident ticket noting recurring micro-seq tail spikes)
- Confluence: serving-runtime/prefetching-diary (background on previous prefetch tuning)

End of notes.

(Handy: tagging this with "in_review" until we finish trace replays — will flip to "final" after E1/E2 complete.)
